solution: The tropopause is highest over the equator (tall, warm equatorial troposphere) and acts as a barrier to the vertical movement of air, so statements 1 and 2 are correct. Its height varies seasonally, so statement 3 is wrong. Answer: A.

The troposphere is heated from below by the Earth's surface. With altitude the air pressure and density fall, so the air retains less heat and cools. Distance from the Sun is effectively unchanged, so that option is wrong. Answer: A.
From the surface upward the layers are Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere. Answer: A.

The Coriolis force is zero at the Equator and increases towards the Poles, so 1 and 2 are correct. It deflects the direction of wind but does not determine wind speed (that is set by the pressure gradient), so 3 is wrong. Answer: A.
Meteors burn up in the Mesosphere, where the air is dense enough to cause frictional heating. Answer: B.
Albedo is the fraction of incoming solar radiation that is reflected by a surface or by the Earth. Answer: B.
The upper atmosphere (thermosphere) is heated by direct absorption of high-energy ultraviolet and X-ray radiation from the Sun. Answer: B.
Methane, carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide are greenhouse gases; nitrogen is not. Answer: D.
About three-quarters of the atmosphere's mass lies in the Troposphere. Answer: A.
Nitrogen (~78%) is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere. Answer: C.
The exosphere is dominated by the lightest gases; hydrogen (with helium) is present in the highest quantity. Answer: A.
Oxygen (~21%) is the second most abundant atmospheric gas after nitrogen. Answer: A.
Oxygen makes up about 21% of the atmosphere. Answer: B.
From the surface upward: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere. Answer: B.
The normal lapse rate ceases (temperature stops falling) at the top of the troposphere, i.e. the tropopause. Answer: B.
All weather phenomena (clouds, rain, storms) occur in the Troposphere, which holds the water vapour and dust. Answer: B.

The troposphere is thickest over the equator (1 correct). The tropopause is coldest over the equator and warmer over the poles, so its temperature is highest above the poles (2 correct). The normal lapse rate is about 1°C (not 1°F) per ~165 m, so 3 is wrong. Answer: B.
In the troposphere temperature decreases with height at the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per kilometre. Answer: D.
Dark tropical forest has a low albedo; replacing it with lighter agricultural land raises the surface reflectivity, so albedo increases. Answer: C.
Water vapour, methane and ozone are greenhouse gases; carbon monoxide is not a direct greenhouse gas. Answer: D.
A higher albedo means more solar radiation is reflected and less absorbed, so the Earth's surface cools. Answer: C.
The atmosphere is heated chiefly by longwave terrestrial radiation emitted by the Earth, not directly by incoming solar radiation. Answer: C.
Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases; oxygen is not. Answer: B.
By Rayleigh scattering, shorter-wavelength blue light is scattered much more than red, which is why the sky appears blue. Answer: A.
Dense forest is dark and absorbs most radiation, giving it the lowest albedo of the options (snow, clouds and desert are all brighter). Answer: C.

Albedo influences Earth's energy balance (1 correct) and extensive ice cover raises planetary albedo (2 correct). Deforestation usually increases albedo, so 'always decreases' is wrong (3). Answer: A.
Fresh snow cover reflects most incident radiation and has the highest albedo (~0.8-0.9). Answer: C.
Clouds form in the Troposphere, the layer containing water vapour and weather. Answer: A.
The Coriolis force increases with wind velocity (1 correct) and is maximum at the poles and absent at the equator (2 correct). Answer: C.

Incoming solar radiation is mostly visible/shortwave (S1 true) and terrestrial radiation is mostly longwave infrared (S2 true). The atmosphere is more transparent to incoming solar and absorbs terrestrial longwave, so S3 is false. Answer: A.

The atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial longwave radiation than by incoming solar, so S1 is incorrect. CO2 and greenhouse gases are good absorbers of longwave radiation, so S2 is correct. Answer: D.
Insolation is predominantly shortwave radiation (S1 true), but it is unevenly distributed with latitude (S2 false). Answer: A.
Fresh snow has the highest albedo of the listed surfaces. Answer: A.

Temperature rises with height in the stratosphere (S1) and falls in the mesosphere (S2); the lowest atmospheric temperature occurs near the mesopause / upper mesosphere (S3); and the tropopause is an isothermal zone (S4). All four are correct. Answer: D.
Isotherms are lines joining places of equal temperature. Answer: C.

Most atmospheric water vapour is concentrated in the lowest layers (statement 1 taken as correct). Precipitable water decreases — not increases — from equator to pole, so statement 2 is wrong. Answer: A.
Ultraviolet rays are absorbed mainly by the ozone layer in the Stratosphere, shielding the surface. Answer: D.
Jet streams are fast upper-air winds found near the Tropopause. Answer: C.
The highest concentration of water vapour is in the troposphere, not the stratosphere, so that statement is NOT correct. The other statements about the stratosphere are true. Answer: D.

Statement 1 is false (the atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial longwave than by incoming solar). Statement 2 is true: CO2 and water vapour transmit incoming solar but absorb outgoing terrestrial radiation. Answer: B.

Insolation is the incoming solar radiation received at the surface (S1 true), and maximum insolation falls on the cloud-free subtropical deserts (S2 true). S3 is false — the 'proximity to the Sun' reasoning is wrong and it is the deserts, not the equator, that get maximum insolation. Answer: A.
Albedo is the reflected fraction of radiation (S1 true) and Venus has the highest albedo among planetary bodies (S2 true). Fresh snow has a higher albedo than old snow, so S3 is false. Answer: B.
Conduction is heat transfer by direct contact (S1 true) and convection is vertical heating by rising air (S2 true). Advection is the HORIZONTAL transfer of heat, so S3 is false. Answer: A.

The Earth radiates absorbed insolation back as longwave radiation (S1 true), which greenhouse gases absorb (S2 true). The atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial than by solar radiation, so S3 is false. Answer: A.

The troposphere extends ~18 km at the equator and ~8 km at the poles (S1), is the densest layer with dust and water vapour (S2), and cools at the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C/km (S3). All three are correct. Answer: D.

The stratosphere extends ~18-50 km (S1) and is ideal for aircraft due to the absence of weather disturbances (S2). The maximum-ozone layer is the ozonosphere, not the 'Mesopause', so S3 is false. Answer: B.
The mesosphere reaches ~80 km and is the coldest layer (S1), meteors burn up here (S2), and noctilucent clouds form here over the poles in summer (S3). All three are correct. Answer: D.

The thermosphere/ionosphere reflects radio waves (S1 true) and the ISS and satellites orbit within it (S3 true). S2 is false — Aurora Borealis is in the Northern Hemisphere and Aurora Australis in the Southern (the statement swaps them). Answer: B.

The Coriolis force is an apparent force due to Earth's rotation (S1 true) that deflects motion right in the Northern and left in the Southern Hemisphere (S2 true). It is maximum at the poles and zero at the equator, so S3 (which swaps them) is false. Answer: B.

Nitrogen ~78% and oxygen ~21% by volume (S1), about 99% of the atmosphere's mass lies within ~32 km of the surface (S2), and radon anomalies are studied for earthquake prediction (S3). All three are correct. Answer: D.
